strengths: Addresses a timely and underexplored problem: safety vulnerabilities specific to diffusion-based LLMs (dLLMs), an emerging architecture class.

Clear, mechanistically-grounded threat model tying the attack to two genuine architectural properties of dLLMs (bidirectional context modeling and parallel decoding), rather than a generic prompt-engineering trick.

Comprehensive empirical evaluation across four dLLM families (LLaDA, LLaDA-1.5, Dream, MMaDA) and three established jailbreak benchmarks (HarmBench, JailbreakBench, StrongREJECT), using multiple complementary metrics (ASR-k, ASR-e, HS, SRS).

Strong and consistent quantitative improvements over multiple existing jailbreak baselines (AIM, PAIR, ReNeLLM), including near-100% ASR in several settings, with numbers that appear large enough to be meaningful rather than marginal.
Includes robustness checks against two representative defenses (Self-reminder, RPO) and an ablation on masking granularity/length that supports the proposed mechanistic explanation.
Automated, scalable attack pipeline (no manual prompt rewriting or content obfuscation) that could generalize easily to new dLLMs, aiding reproducibility.
Reasonably thorough appendix with implementation details, prompt templates, and judge prompts, supporting reproducibility of the reported numbers.
weaknesses: The central insight - that forcing completion of masked spans embedded in an already-harmful, unmasked context will elicit harmful continuations - is somewhat intuitive; the paper's novelty is mainly in systematizing and automating this observation rather than a fundamentally new algorithmic or theoretical contribution.

Evaluation relies heavily on GPT-4o as both the harmful-score judge and (for DIJA*) the prompt-refinement model, with no human validation of judgment quality or inter-rater agreement, raising concerns about evaluator bias and consistency.

Baseline attacks (AIM, PAIR, ReNeLLM) were designed for autoregressive LLMs and are applied to dLLMs without adaptation to the mask-based interface, making the comparison somewhat unfair or orthogonal rather than a matched comparison of attack paradigms.

Only two generic, non-dLLM-specific defenses are tested (Self-reminder, RPO); since no dLLM-tailored defenses exist yet, the robustness-against-defenses claim is only weakly informative about worst-case mitigability.

Limited model diversity (4 dLLMs, all masked-diffusion variants) restricts generality claims; larger or differently-trained dLLMs are not evaluated, though this is partially acknowledged as future work.

The explanation for generation-length and mask-count effects in Section 5 is largely a post-hoc qualitative hypothesis without rigorous causal analysis (e.g., attention pattern analysis) of why bidirectional attention specifically drives this failure mode.

Ethical and dual-use concerns: the fully automated, high-success-rate jailbreak pipeline is released with limited discussion of responsible disclosure or concrete mitigation strategies beyond generic calls for future alignment work.

strengths: Identifies a timely and plausible new attack surface specific to diffusion LLMs (dLLMs), tying the vulnerability to concrete architectural properties (bidirectional context modeling and parallel decoding) rather than generic prompt engineering.

Reasonably broad empirical coverage: four dLLM families (LLaDA, LLaDA-1.5, Dream, MMaDA) evaluated on three jailbreak benchmarks (HarmBench, JailbreakBench, StrongREJECT) with multiple metrics (ASR-k, ASR-e, HS, SRS).

The attack pipeline is fully automated (via in-context learning with an auxiliary LLM) and requires no manual rewriting or obfuscation of harmful content, which is a meaningful practical advantage over baselines like ReNeLLM/PAIR for demonstrating the severity of the issue.

Includes some robustness checks against two existing jailbreak defenses and an auxiliary analysis of the effect of generation length/number of masked tokens, offering a bit of mechanistic insight into why the attack works.
Honest discussion of limitations (no white-box baselines, limited model set) in the appendix.
weaknesses: No proposed mitigation or defense tailored to dLLMs; the paper is purely an attack demonstration with a generic call to 'rethink alignment,' limiting its constructive contribution to the field.

Evaluation relies heavily on GPT-4o as both the automated prompt-refinement model (in DIJA*) and the judge for ASR-e/HS, raising concerns about circularity and judge bias; no human evaluation is used to validate the reliability of keyword-based or LLM-judged ASR, despite keyword-based ASR being known to overestimate attack success.

The core mechanism—forcing completion of masked slots to elicit harmful content—is a fairly natural extension of known fill-in-the-blank/decomposition-style jailbreaks (e.g., DrAttack) applied to a new architecture, so the claimed novelty of 'first systematic study' may be somewhat overstated relative to the conceptual leap required.

Mechanistic analysis is shallow: claims about why alignment fails on masked-interleaved prompts (e.g., whether safety training simply never saw masked-prompt distributions) are asserted but not empirically tested (e.g., via probing, attention analysis, or targeted fine-tuning on masked refusal data).

Only two generic, AR-oriented defenses (Self-reminder, RPO) are tested; no exploration of simple, plausible dLLM-specific mitigations (e.g., detecting/limiting mask density, safety-aware remasking, restricting block-wise unmasking of long harmful spans) that would make the paper's security contribution more actionable.

Inconsistent/counterintuitive results (e.g., MMaDA showing weaker defensibility even under zero-shot while other models show near-zero ASR, and AIM performing essentially at the noise floor) are not sufficiently analyzed or explained, leaving open questions about whether baseline comparisons are entirely fair (e.g., gen_length/hyperparameters fixed across very different attack styles).
Single-run results with no variance/confidence intervals reported, and limited qualitative error analysis of borderline or failed cases beyond a handful of cherry-picked success examples in Figure 4.

strengths: Identifies a genuinely novel and timely safety vulnerability class specific to diffusion LLMs (dLLMs), rooted in a clear mechanistic explanation (bidirectional context modeling + parallel decoding breaking rejection sampling), which is well-motivated and not merely a superficial restatement of existing jailbreak techniques.

Comprehensive empirical evaluation across multiple representative dLLM families (LLaDA, LLaDA-1.5, Dream, MMaDA) and three established jailbreak benchmarks (HarmBench, JailbreakBench, StrongREJECT), with multiple complementary metrics (ASR-k, ASR-e, HS, SRS).

Strong and consistent performance gains over multiple relevant baselines (AIM, PAIR, ReNeLLM), including large margins in evaluator-based ASR and StrongREJECT score, and notably without needing to obfuscate or hide harmful intent in the prompt, which is itself an interesting and concerning finding.
Includes robustness checks against two defense mechanisms (Self-reminder, RPO) showing the attack is not trivially mitigated by existing prompt-based defenses.
Useful auxiliary analyses (effect of generation length, effect of number of masked tokens) that provide some mechanistic insight into why the attack works and its sensitivity to design parameters.

The paper is clearly written with illustrative figures/examples that make the attack mechanism easy to understand, and the appendix provides good reproducibility detail (prompts, templates, keyword lists, judge prompts).
weaknesses: The attack construction pipeline relies heavily on an external LLM (Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct or GPT-4o) to generate the interleaved mask-text prompts via in-context learning; this introduces an external dependency and makes 'DIJA' less a standalone systematic algorithm and more an LLM-assisted prompting strategy, which could affect reproducibility and makes attribution of effectiveness (attack design vs. underlying LLM's creativity) less clean.

No white-box or gradient-based baselines (e.g., GCG) are included, which the authors acknowledge; this leaves open whether the vulnerability is fundamentally different from known failure modes or simply another prompt-engineering jailbreak optimized for a new architecture.

Harmfulness evaluation relies solely on GPT-4o as judge without any human verification/inter-rater agreement check, which is a common but still notable limitation given known biases and inconsistencies of LLM-based judges.

Defense evaluation is limited to two relatively simple prompt-level defenses (Self-reminder, RPO); no exploration of defenses tailored to the masked/parallel decoding setting (e.g., confidence-based remasking filters, selective re-ranking, or fine-tuning-based mitigations), leaving the practical difficulty of patching this vulnerability underexplored.

The number-of-masked-tokens and generation-length ablations show non-monotonic effects that are described only informally/anecdotally (via hypothesis) without deeper theoretical or mechanistic analysis of why bidirectional attention produces this trend.

Scope is restricted to text-only dLLMs; while future work is acknowledged, the claimed generality of the vulnerability to the broader class of non-autoregressive architectures (including multimodal dLLMs) is not empirically substantiated in this paper.

strengths: Identifies a novel and timely safety concern specific to diffusion LLMs (dLLMs), an emerging and increasingly popular model class, filling a genuine gap in the jailbreak literature which has focused almost exclusively on autoregressive LLMs.

The proposed mechanism (interleaved mask-text prompts exploiting bidirectional context modeling and parallel decoding) is well motivated and tied concretely to architectural properties unique to dLLMs, rather than being a generic prompt-engineering trick.

Extensive empirical evaluation across multiple dLLM families (LLaDA, Dream, MMaDA, DiffuCoder, Dream-Coder) and three jailbreak benchmarks (HarmBench, JailbreakBench, StrongREJECT), with consistently large improvements over strong baselines (ReNeLLM, PAIR, GCG, AIM).

Thorough ablation and robustness studies: component ablations (masking vs. separators vs. refinement LLM), mask span/length sensitivity analysis, reproducibility/stability across seeds and temperatures, and evaluation under two defense mechanisms (Self-reminder, RPO).
Includes a human validation study of the GPT-4o harmfulness judge (high Cohen's kappa and Pearson correlation), strengthening confidence in the automated evaluation metrics.

Provides a preliminary architecture-aware defense (Refusal-Aware Denoising Alignment) that substantially reduces attack success while largely preserving general capability, demonstrating the vulnerability is at least partially addressable.
Good reproducibility commitments (code, alignment data, model weights to be released) and a thoughtful discussion of threat model assumptions and relation to prefilling attacks in the appendix.
weaknesses: The core attack requires the attacker to control the structure/masking of the model's response (i.e., dictate which spans are 'assistant-generated' vs fixed), which is a fundamentally different and stronger threat model than standard jailbreak baselines (PAIR, GCG, AIM, ReNeLLM) that only control the input prompt; comparing ASR/HS numbers across these different threat models is somewhat apples-to-oranges and could overstate the attack's relative advantage.

The attack closely resembles known prefilling/response-control attacks on autoregressive models (as the paper itself acknowledges in Appendix B.7), so the core insight is arguably an adaptation of an existing attack class to a new architecture rather than a fundamentally new vulnerability, tempering the novelty claim of 'first investigation.'

Many illustrative examples (Figure 2, Figure 4) already embed most of the harmful intent explicitly in the fixed/unmasked text (e.g., naming the harmful topic in full), so the model's job is largely to elaborate on an already-stated harmful request; this raises the question of how much the 'vulnerability' differs from simply not refusing an already-graphic prompt versus a genuinely emergent architectural flaw.

The practical applicability of the threat model to real-world closed-source dLLM deployments is uncertain and mostly speculative (the paper concedes current commercial APIs largely lack exposed masking/infilling endpoints), which somewhat limits the immediate real-world significance of the findings.

The defense proposed (Refusal-Aware Denoising Alignment) is trained and evaluated only against the same DIJA-style attack it was designed to counter (in-distribution), with no evaluation against unseen masking patterns/paraphrased attacks, leaving open whether the fix generalizes rather than overfits to the specific pattern.

Some presentation issues: heavy reliance on GPT-4o as both attack-prompt generator and evaluator could introduce judge bias/correlation effects not fully explored beyond the limited 100-sample human check.

strengths: Identifies a genuinely interesting and timely research question: whether the bidirectional, parallel-decoding nature of dLLMs creates safety vulnerabilities distinct from autoregressive LLMs.

Reasonably broad empirical evaluation across multiple dLLM families (LLaDA, Dream, MMaDA, DiffuCoder) and three jailbreak benchmarks (HarmBench, JailbreakBench, StrongREJECT), with several complementary metrics (ASR-k, ASR-e, HS, SRS).

Includes a fairly extensive appendix with ablations (masking vs. separators vs. refinement LLM), mask-span/length sensitivity analysis, reproducibility/stability checks, and a human validation of the GPT-4o judge, which adds some rigor beyond the headline numbers.
Attempts a preliminary architecture-aware defense (refusal-aware denoising alignment) rather than only presenting an attack, which is a constructive contribution direction.
The qualitative examples (Figure 2, Figure 4) are illustrative and make the phenomenon concrete.
weaknesses: The core threat model is questionable: DIJA requires the attacker to directly insert [MASK] tokens at arbitrary positions into the model's input/output, which is a highly privileged and non-standard interface not available to typical end users of a chat-style dLLM product; this is fundamentally different from—and much stronger than—the black-box prompting threat model used by essentially all baseline jailbreak methods (PAIR, GCG, AIM, ReNeLLM), making the headline comparisons (e.g., '78.5% higher ASR-e than ReNeLLM') somewhat apples-to-oranges rather than a fair demonstration of a new 'vulnerability.'

The paper's own appendix (B.7) concedes that the attack only applies when a remasking/infilling API is exposed, yet the main text repeatedly frames this as an 'emergent safety vulnerability' and 'critical gap' in current alignment without adequately foregrounding this strong assumption in the abstract/introduction, which risks overstating the practical severity of the threat.

Technical novelty is limited: the method is essentially (a) wrap a harmful instruction with mask tokens and benign connective text, and (b) use an LLM with few-shot ICL to automate this templating. The 'factorization' argument in Eq. 6 is a restatement of how masked diffusion decoding works rather than a new theoretical insight, and the three 'strategies' (diversification, masking pattern selection, separator insertion) are engineering heuristics rather than a principled or learned attack.

Claims of being the 'first investigation into the safety issues of dLLMs' and 'first systematic jailbreak attack framework' are strong claims that are not rigorously substantiated against the broader jailbreak/red-teaming literature on non-autoregressive or infilling models, and such superlative framing is somewhat risky/overclaiming for a paper whose main technical trick is prompt templating plus mask insertion.

Keyword-based ASR (ASR-k), prominently reported as reaching up to 100%, is a well-known unreliable metric (acknowledged by the authors' own citations, e.g., StrongREJECT motivation) and its heavy use alongside ASR-e inflates the apparent strength of results in the abstract.

The defense evaluation is narrow: only two generic prompt-based defenses (self-reminder, RPO) are tested, which are not dLLM-specific; there is no comparison against an adapted or dLLM-aware baseline defense (e.g., detecting anomalous mask patterns, limiting mask span counts/positions at the system level), which would be a natural and fairer test of the claimed vulnerability's robustness.

The proposed refusal-aware denoising alignment fix is only validated on a single model (LLaDA-8B-Instruct) and against the authors' own attack distribution; there is no test of generalization to unseen masking patterns, different mask densities, or other victim architectures (Dream, MMaDA), making the 'alignment is possible' claim weakly supported.

Several related-works/positioning statements and the abstract's rhetoric ('urgent need,' 'critical vulnerability,' 'immediate addressing') are somewhat alarmist relative to the actual demonstrated scope (requires API-level mask access), which may raise concerns about calibration of claims versus evidence.

The human validation of the harmfulness judge (N=100) is a reasonable sanity check but is applied only to DIJA outputs, not to baseline outputs, so it does not establish that the comparative gaps between DIJA and baselines are judge-reliable rather than judge-biased.

strengths: Identifies a novel, architecture-specific safety vulnerability in diffusion LLMs (dLLMs) grounded in their bidirectional context modeling and parallel decoding mechanisms, which is a timely and underexplored topic as dLLMs gain traction.

Comprehensive empirical evaluation across multiple dLLM families (LLaDA, Dream, MMaDA, plus code-oriented dLLMs like DiffuCoder and Dream-Coder) and three jailbreak benchmarks (HarmBench, JailbreakBench, StrongREJECT), with strong and consistent improvements over competitive baselines (GCG, AIM, PAIR, ReNeLLM).

Extensive ablation studies (removing refinement LLM, masking mechanism, separators; varying mask span count and token budget) convincingly isolate that the attack's effectiveness stems from the interleaved mask-text structure itself rather than auxiliary prompt engineering, strengthening the causal claim about dLLM-specific vulnerabilities.

Strong reproducibility practices: detailed algorithm pseudocode, multiple independent runs with varying temperature showing low variance, human validation of the GPT-4o harmfulness judge (high Cohen's kappa and Pearson correlation), and a stated commitment to release code, data, and model weights.

Goes beyond attack demonstration by proposing a preliminary architecture-aware defense (Refusal-Aware Denoising Alignment) and showing it substantially reduces attack success with limited degradation on general benchmarks, adding constructive value.

Robustness checks against existing defenses (Self-reminder, RPO) and thoughtful discussion of threat model assumptions and relation to prefilling attacks demonstrate rigor and self-awareness of scope/limitations.
weaknesses: The evaluator-based ASR (ASR-e), arguably the more meaningful metric, is lower than keyword-based ASR and in some cases comparable to or only moderately better than ReNeLLM (e.g., HarmBench on LLaDA-Instruct: 55.5% vs ReNeLLM's... actually higher but with some benchmarks the gap is less dramatic than headline numbers suggest), and it would help to more clearly contextualize where gains are modest versus large.

The paper positions DIJA against existing autoregressive-targeted baselines as if this is a fair apples-to-apples comparison, but since DIJA exploits a fundamentally different capability (editable/maskable input) not available to the baselines nor assumed in their threat model, the comparison somewhat overstates DIJA's relative advantage rather than reflecting genuinely comparable attack surfaces.

The threat model assumption (attacker can insert/control mask token placement within the prompt, effectively dictating output structure) is relatively strong and may not generalize to realistic closed/served dLLM deployments where such fine-grained mask control is not exposed, somewhat limiting real-world applicability versus the dramatic framing in the abstract/intro.

The refusal-aware denoising alignment defense, while a nice addition, is only tested on a single model (LLaDA-8B-Instruct) and may itself be attackable by adaptive adversaries (e.g., slightly perturbing the interleaving pattern), which is not explored.

Some presentation redundancy (e.g., repeated reference lists, duplicated PAIR citation entries) and the main paper leans heavily on the appendix for key robustness/ablation evidence, which could be better integrated or summarized in the main text.
